Dataset title: National Health Interview Survey
Organization/publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (NCHS)

# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

messages.content:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: National Health Interview Survey
Organization/publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (NCHS)
Description: The National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) monitors the health of the U.S. population by collecting and analyzing data on a broad range of health topics for children and adults. Conducted by CDC's National Center for Health Statistics, it is the nation's largest and oldest national health survey, collecting data since 1957 from about 27,000 adults each year through confidential, face-to-face interviews.
URL: https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhis/index.html

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

I'll research the National Health Interview Survey comprehensively, verifying the details you've provided and digging deeper into each aspect.I have solid confirmation of the statutory basis and history. Now let me research data access mechanisms, confidentiality protections, and recent developments affecting the survey.# National Health Interview Survey (NHIS): Comprehensive Research Report

## 1. Verification of Your Stated Facts

Your information is **substantially accurate**, with a few refinements worth noting:

| Your claim | Verification |
|---|---|
| **Title: National Health Interview Survey** | ✅ Correct. |
| **Publisher: CDC / NCHS** | ✅ Correct. The survey is administered by the Division of Health Interview Statistics (DHIS) within the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS), part of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). |
| **Data collection since 1957** | ✅ Correct — in the field continuously since **July 1957**, making it the nation's oldest ongoing household-based health survey. |
| **~27,000 adults annually** | ✅ Correct for the current (post-2019) design: roughly 27,000–30,000 "Sample Adult" and ~8,000–9,000 "Sample Child" interviews from ~30,000–35,000 households. ⚠️ Note: under the pre-2019 design, NHIS interviewed *all* household members (~87,500–100,000 people in ~35,000–45,000 households), so historical sample sizes are much larger. |
| **Face-to-face interviews** | ⚠️ Mostly correct historically. The primary mode is in-person computer-assisted personal interviewing (CAPI) by U.S. Census Bureau field representatives, with telephone follow-up. During COVID-19 (2020–2021), NHIS shifted substantially to telephone-first interviewing, and it now operates as a mixed-mode survey. |
| **URL: cdc.gov/nchs/nhis/index.html** | ✅ Correct landing page. |

---

## 2. Publisher, Authority, and Legal Mandate

### Organizational home
- **Administering unit:** Division of Health Interview Statistics (DHIS), NCHS, CDC, HHS.
- **Data collector:** The **U.S. Census Bureau** conducts interviews under an interagency agreement, authorized by Title 13, U.S.C., Section 8(b). Census field representatives handle sampling, frame construction, and interviewing.

### Statutory authority
- **National Health Survey Act of 1956** — provided for "a continuing survey and special studies to secure accurate and current statistical information on the amount, distribution, and effects of illness and disability in the United States." This is the direct legislative origin of NHIS.
- **Section 306 of the Public Health Service Act (42 U.S.C. § 242k)** — the standing mandate establishing NCHS and directing it to collect statistics on the extent and nature of illness and disability, determinants of health, health care utilization, costs and financing, and related topics. This is the citation to use when referencing NHIS's authority.
- **Paperwork Reduction Act / OMB clearance** — like all federal surveys, NHIS content is cleared through OMB and announced via Federal Register notices (useful for tracking upcoming questionnaire changes).

### Confidentiality protections (critical for users and preservationists)
- **Section 308(d) of the PHS Act (42 U.S.C. § 242m(d))** and **CIPSEA (Confidential Information Protection and Statistical Efficiency Act, enacted via the Foundations for Evidence-Based Policymaking Act of 2018, 44 U.S.C. §§ 3561–3583)** guarantee that data are used *only* for statistical purposes. CIPSEA violations are a **Class E felony** (up to 5 years imprisonment, $250,000 fine).
- Public-use files are disclosure-protected: state identifiers and fine geography are suppressed, strata and PSUs are masked, variables are coarsened, and statistical noise may be added. Detailed versions are available only through the **NCHS Research Data Center (RDC)** under approved applications.

---

## 3. History and Evolution

- **1956:** National Health Survey Act passed.
- **July 1957:** NHIS fielded continuously ever since — over 65 years without interruption.
- **1960:** The National Health Survey merged with the National Vital Statistics Division to form NCHS, which has conducted the survey since.
- **Decennial sample redesigns:** The sample is redesigned after each Census (most recent design: 2016–2025).
- **Major questionnaire revisions (~every 10–15 years):** notably **1982**, **1997** (major redesign introducing CAPI and a "sample adult/sample child + family core" structure), and **January 2019** (the first full redesign in over 20 years).
- **The 2019 redesign** is the single most important structural fact for modern users:
  - Reduced respondents per household to **one Sample Adult (18+)** and **one Sample Child (0–17)**, randomly selected after a household roster.
  - Restructured content into an **annual core**, **rotating core**, and **sponsored modules** (other HHS agencies can buy question space — e.g., cancer screening, epilepsy, caregiving, occupational health, loneliness/isolation).
  - Revised wording, harmonized with other federal surveys, and changed weighting/nonresponse adjustments — creating a **trend break**: NCHS explicitly cautions that 2018→2019 differences may reflect redesign artifacts, not real change.
- **COVID-19 era:** Shifted to telephone-first contact; response rates and composition shifted; NCHS published extensive evaluations.
- **2025 disruption:** During the October–November 2025 lapse in appropriations, Census Bureau data collection paused (Oct 1–Nov 16), restarting Nov 18; the 2025 field period extended into January 2026.

---

## 4. Survey Design and Methodology

- **Population:** Civilian, noninstitutionalized U.S. population (excludes active-duty military, institutionalized persons such as nursing home residents and prisoners — an important coverage limitation).
- **Design:** Cross-sectional, continuous, annual; geographically clustered, stratified multistage area probability sample covering all 50 states and DC.
- **Size (current design):** ~30,000–35,000 households; ~27,000 Sample Adult + ~8,000–9,000 Sample Child interviews annually. Sample size flexes with budget and supplemental funding; analysts routinely pool 2+ years for subgroup estimates.
- **Response:** Self-response for Sample Adults (proxy allowed if physically/mentally unable); a knowledgeable parent/adult answers for Sample Children.
- **Content domains:** health status and chronic conditions, mental health, functioning and disability (Washington Group questions), health insurance coverage, access to and use of care, immunizations, health behaviors (tobacco, alcohol, physical activity, diet), injuries, occupational health, demographics and socioeconomic characteristics.
- **Weights and variance:** Public files include final annual weights and **masked** variance strata/PSUs for Taylor linearization; NCHS publishes PRICSSA-aligned analytic guidelines (Preferred Reporting Items for Complex Sample Survey Analysis).

---

## 5. Data Products and Access Points

### Public-use files (free, immediate download)
- Annual files from the NHIS website and the **CDC FTP archive** (ftp.cdc.gov → Health_Statistics/NCHS): ASCII and CSV data with **SAS, SPSS, and Stata** input statements, plus questionnaires, survey descriptions, and codebooks. Historical files are retained in this archive.
- **Early Release Program:** preliminary estimates of ~15 key indicators (e.g., uninsurance) released months before final files. Note: as of 2025, *quarterly* estimates were discontinued in favor of a **biannual release** schedule.
- **data.cdc.gov (Socrata API):** selected NHIS tables and the Public-Use Linked Mortality Files, with API endpoints useful for automated monitoring and preservation harvesting.

### Linked data
- **NHIS–National Death Index Linked Mortality Files:** public-use files (NHIS 1986–2018, with perturbation for disclosure protection; follow-up through 2019 for that release) and restricted-use files (updated through Dec 31, 2022) via the RDC. These enable prospective mortality-outcome research from survey data.
- **NCHS–CMS linkage:** Medicare enrollment/claims/Part D and Medicaid data linked to NHIS respondents (restricted-use, RDC only); public "feasibility files" help researchers assess suitability.

### Restricted data
- Via the **NCHS Research Data Center** (Hyattsville, MD; Census FSRDC network; and remote access): state/county geography, unsuppressed variables, and linked files. Requires proposal approval; disclosure review of outputs.

### Third-party harmonized archives (important for preservation)
- **IPUMS NHIS (IPUMS Health Surveys, University of Minnesota):** free, harmonized NHIS microdata from **1963 to present**, with 17,000+ consistently coded variables, integrated documentation of comparability issues, an extract system, online tabulator, and integrated linked-mortality data. Collection-level DOI: 10.18128/C070. This is the de facto longitudinal preservation and usability layer for NHIS, and a key redundancy if federal distribution is disrupted.

---

## 6. Typical Users

- **HHS and federal agencies:** NHIS is described by NCHS as "the single most important source of statistics to track progress toward HHS health objectives" — it feeds **Healthy People 2030** objectives and the congressionally mandated **Health, United States** report. NHIS respondents also serve as the sampling frame for AHRQ's **Medical Expenditure Panel Survey (MEPS)**, tying NHIS into the broader federal health data ecosystem.
- **Congress and policy analysts:** NHIS is a **gold-standard source on health insurance coverage and uninsurance**, heavily used to evaluate the Affordable Care Act, Medicaid policy, and access-to-care legislation.
- **Academic and private researchers:** epidemiology, health services research, health disparities, disability studies, child health; thousands of publications (the IPUMS bibliography tracks them).
- **State and local public health** (limited by the suppression of sub-state geography in public files).
- **Journalists and advocates** tracking uninsurance, chronic disease prevalence, and health behaviors.

---

## 7. Public Benefits

1. **National health surveillance:** the principal source on illness, disability, and health status for the U.S. population, enabling trend analysis back to 1957 (1963 in harmonized digital form).
2. **Accountability infrastructure:** underpins Healthy People targets, HHS strategic objectives, and congressional reporting — you can't manage what you can't measure.
3. **Policy evaluation:** definitive uninsurance and coverage estimates used to assess the ACA, Medicaid expansion, and pandemic-era coverage policies.
4. **Equity analysis:** ability to disaggregate health outcomes by race/ethnicity, income, education, and other demographics makes it a core tool for health-disparities research.
5. **Scientific leverage via linkage:** NHIS-NDI and NHIS-CMS linkages convert a cross-sectional survey into a longitudinal research platform at near-zero marginal cost to respondents.
6. **Efficiency of open access:** free public-use microdata (plus IPUMS harmonization) multiply the return on taxpayer investment thousands-fold through secondary research.

---

## 8. Preservation, Technical, and Risk Notes (for archivists, librarians, data scientists)

**Known data quirks and limitations:**
- **Trend breaks:** 1997 and especially **2019** redesigns break comparability; always consult NCHS evaluation reports and IPUMS comparability documentation before pooling across breaks.
- **Coverage gaps:** excludes institutionalized and military populations.
- **Confidentiality edits:** masked design variables, coarsened geography, possible noise infusion — reproduce estimates using the provided weights and masked variance units.
- **Variable churn:** rotating and sponsored content means many variables exist only in selected years.

**Current risks to continuity (2025–present):**
- **Staffing shocks:** NCHS lost ~10% of staff by fall 2025; in October 2025, ~110 NCHS employees (~25% of the workforce) received RIF notices during the government shutdown — rescinded by mid-November 2025 as part of the shutdown-ending deal, but the episode exposed fragility (documented in the *American Journal of Public Health* and the American Statistical Association's "Nation's Data at Risk" reports).
- **Budget pressure:** NCHS has lost ~16% of purchasing power since FY2009; the FY26 President's Budget proposed further staffing decline; the median requested annual budget increase for NCHS over 2001–2025 was 0.1% — the lowest of all 13 principal statistical agencies.
- **Reorganization proposal:** HHS has proposed moving NCHS out of CDC into a new office under the HHS Secretary — implications for statistical-agency independence are contested.
- **Operational impacts already visible:** quarterly Early Release estimates discontinued (moved to biannual); the 2025 field period was disrupted by the shutdown; ended contracts have weakened report production and data release capacity.
- **Preservation implication:** Because effects of 2025 cuts may lag 12+ months into releases, now is a prudent time to mirror the FTP archive, data.cdc.gov endpoints, survey descriptions, questionnaires, and codebooks, and to leverage IPUMS as a redundant, DOI-citable archive.

**Citation:** NCHS requests citation of the specific year's survey description document (e.g., "National Center for Health Statistics. National Health Interview Survey, 2024 [public-use data file and documentation]"). Use the IPUMS DOI (10.18128/C070) for harmonized extracts.

---

## 9. Key Sources Consulted

- NCHS Statutory Authorities page; 42 U.S.C. § 242k (PHS Act §306); Census Bureau NHIS page (Title 13 §8(b))
- NHIS Survey Description documents (2019, 2024, 2025), incl. PRICSSA and confidentiality statements (ftp.cdc.gov)
- CDC 2019 Questionnaire Redesign documentation; Health, United States NHIS source page
- NCHS Data Linkage Program pages (NDI mortality, CMS Medicare, RDC access)
- IPUMS Health Surveys / IPUMS NHIS (University of Minnesota)
- American Statistical Association, "The Nation's Data at Risk: 2025 Report" (NCHS profile); AJPH (2026), "October 2025 Attempted Workforce Reduction Puts US Principal Health Statistics Agency at Risk"; SHADAC federal health survey release tracking
- Federal Register notice on NHIS 2026–2027 content (Aug 2026)

If you'd like, I can go deeper on any single thread — e.g., a year-by-year inventory of archived files for a preservation crawl, the variable-level comparability issues across the 2019 break, or the mechanics of an RDC application.

I'll conduct additional research on the current status of NHIS — its ICR clearance, staffing, funding, recent publication timeliness, and policy changes — before assigning risk levels.I have strong evidence on most categories. Let me check one more dimension — whether questionnaire content (e.g., demographic items) has been altered under administration policy directives, and the status of the 2028 redesign — before finalizing the Policy and Data Quality ratings.# NHIS Risk Assessment

Based on research of the Federal Register, reginfo.gov/omb.report ICR records, CDC/NCHS release schedules, the American Statistical Association's "Nation's Data at Risk" reporting, SHADAC's federal survey tracking, KFF, the Williams Institute, and disability-community comment guidance (HSRI), here is my category-by-category assessment.

---

## 1. Historical Data Availability

**Evidence for each level:**
- *No Known Issue:* Public-use files back to 1963 remain downloadable from the CDC FTP archive (`ftp.cdc.gov/pub/Health_Statistics/NCHS/`) with questionnaires, codebooks, and survey descriptions; IPUMS NHIS provides an independent harmonized archive (1963–present) with a collection DOI. 2024 and 2025 public-use files have been released. No reports of prior-year NHIS files being deleted or altered. Some CDC *webpages* on sexual orientation/gender identity were taken down in early 2025 (later partially restored under court order), but these were topic pages, not NHIS data files — the underlying microdata retain the variables collected in those years.
- *Moderate/High/Gone:* No evidence found of removal of any historical NHIS data files or elements from prior cycles.

**Assessment: No Known Issue.** Historical files remain accessible and unaltered. (Preservation note: mirroring is still prudent given institutional volatility documented below, and because CDC page removals in 2025 showed web content can disappear quickly even when data files survive.)

## 2. Future Data Availability

**Evidence for each level:**
- *No Known Issue:* The ICR (OMB Control No. 0920-0214) is active through 12/31/2026; a nonsubstantive change was approved 01/30/2026; and a full three-year extension for 2027–2029 collection is moving through the normal PRA process (60-day Federal Register notice, Aug 20, 2026). The 2025 annual Early Release estimates published 05/28/2026 and 2025 public-use files released (September 2026) — on the typical schedule. No statutory deadline missed; no cycle skipped.
- *Moderate Risk:* During the October–November 2025 lapse in appropriations, Census Bureau fieldwork for NHIS **paused for roughly six weeks** (Oct 1–Nov 16, 2025), and the 2025 field period had to be extended into January 2026 — a documented delay in collection, even though products ultimately shipped on time. NCHS also ended contracts that weakened report production and data release capacity (ASA "Nation's Data at Risk"). The 2028 redesign introduces execution risk (new self-administered modes, untested at scale for NHIS).
- *High Risk/Gone:* No evidence — collection and publication continue; ICR has not lapsed.

**Assessment: Moderate Risk.** The ICR is healthy and releases have stayed on schedule, but the most recent collection cycle was delayed by the shutdown, and the agency's demonstrated exposure to shutdowns, RIF attempts, and contract losses makes future delays plausible. This is the mild end of Moderate.

## 3. Data Quality

**Evidence for each level:**
- *High Risk (realized reductions):*
  - **Frequency:** NCHS discontinued quarterly Early Release estimates and moved to a **biannual** schedule beginning with 2026 releases (confirmed on the NHIS Early Release pages and SHADAC tracking).
  - **Granularity/content:** **Gender identity questions (and follow-ups) were removed from the 2025 NHIS questionnaire** pursuant to Executive Order 14168, via nonsubstantive OMB change requests (documented by KFF, Williams Institute, SHADAC). Sexual orientation items were retained.
- *Moderate Risk (potential/emerging):* The planned **2028 systemic redesign** (Federal Register, Aug 20, 2026) shifts to web/mail self-administration with a **necessarily shorter questionnaire**; "many of the more detailed questions... fielded annually from 2019 to 2027 are not included," and the rotating-content schedule is being dropped. Disability researchers (HSRI crosswalk) document proposed removal of detailed functioning items (wheelchair/mobility equipment, fatigue, learning, age-of-onset), and note some analyses NCHS publishes today could not be reproduced. Mode change plus shorter instrument also creates a likely **trend break** and undercoverage risk for some populations.
- *No Known Issue:* Not supportable — realized reductions exist, though the core annual public-use files (2019–2025) remain full-detail and on time.

**Assessment: High Risk.** Two reductions are already implemented (early-release frequency; removal of gender identity items), and a substantial further granularity reduction is formally proposed for 2028. The core annual dataset remains intact for now, which keeps this from being more severe, but the rubric's High Risk definition — "reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency" — is met.

## 4. Statutory Context

**Evidence for each level:**
- *No Known Issue:* NHIS rests on explicit statutory authorization — the **National Health Survey Act of 1956** and **Section 306 of the Public Health Service Act (42 U.S.C. § 242k)**, which directs NCHS to collect statistics on the extent, nature, and effects of illness and disability and on health care utilization. NHIS data are **required for implementation of federal programs and mandates**: Healthy People 2030 objectives, HHS strategic and performance reporting, and it serves as the sampling frame for AHRQ's MEPS. There is **no adequate substitute**: BRFSS is state-level telephone data without NHIS's depth; MEPS is expenditure-focused and depends on NHIS; NHANES is small-n examination data.
- *Moderate/High:* Not applicable — the statute doesn't name "NHIS" verbatim, but the mandate is explicit, the survey is the designated vehicle, programmatic uses are numerous, and no alternatives exist.

**Assessment: No Known Issue.** This is NHIS's strongest protective factor — and notably, the statute was cited by both defenders of the survey and by NCHS itself in the 2027–2029 clearance package.

## 5. Staffing and Funding

**Evidence for each level:**
- *Moderate Risk (realized):* NCHS **lost an estimated 10% of staff by fall 2025** (ASA, citing staffing tables) — the bottom of the rubric's 10–39% Moderate band. The **FY26 President's Budget proposed 428 FTEs, a 9% decline** from FY24's 470. Contracts were terminated, "particularly weakening the publication of reports and the release of data" (ASA). NCHS has lost ~16% of purchasing power since FY2009 and had the lowest median budget growth of all 13 principal statistical agencies over 2001–2025.
- *High Risk (attempted, then reversed):* On **October 10, 2025, ~110 NCHS employees (~25% of the workforce) received RIF notices** during the shutdown (AJPH; ASA). All were **rescinded by November 18, 2025** as part of the shutdown-ending deal — so the 25% loss was threatened but not realized. HHS has also proposed **reorganizing NCHS out of CDC** into a new office under the HHS Secretary, a threatened structural/leadership change with contested implications for statistical independence.
- *No Known Issue:* Not supportable — 10% realized loss plus budget erosion.

**Assessment: Moderate Risk.** The realized losses (≈10% staffing, contract terminations, proposed ~9% further FTE cut, reorganization threat) fit the Moderate band. The attempted 25% RIF — though rescinded — demonstrates that High Risk conditions were one court ruling or budget cycle away, and the AJPH analysis explicitly frames the agency as fragile.

## 6. Policy

**Evidence for each level:**
- *High Risk:* **Presidential Action-driven changes to the ICR have already occurred.** Under **Executive Order 14168** (Jan 2025), NCHS/CDC specifically cited the EO when requesting OMB approval (via nonsubstantive change requests) to **remove gender identity questions from the 2025 NHIS** (KFF; Williams Institute, which found 83% of such federal removals were processed as nonsubstantive changes, bypassing notice-and-comment). Separately, thousands of CDC/HHS webpages were pulled under administration directives in early 2025 (some restored under court order), showing the agency's dissemination layer is subject to direct political intervention.
- *Moderate Risk:* Also applicable in parallel — the proposed 2028 redesign is a pending change open for comment, and administration officials' reorganization plans for NCHS are pending.
- *No Known Issue:* Not supportable — notable administration-priority-driven changes affecting what NHIS collects have occurred since January 2025.

**Assessment: High Risk.** The rubric's High Risk criterion — "Presidential Action-driven information collection request... other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities" — is directly met by the EO 14168-driven removal of gender identity content from NHIS. The survey itself has not been terminated, but the instrument has already been altered to conform to administration priorities, and the mechanism used (nonsubstantive change requests) allows further such changes with minimal public process.

## Summary of Risk Levels

| Category | Risk Level | One-line rationale |
|---|---|---|
| **Historical Data Availability** | **No Known Issue** | Files back to 1963 intact on CDC FTP and IPUMS; no removals or alterations found |
| **Future Data Availability** | **Moderate Risk** | ICR active and releases on time, but 2025 collection was paused ~6 weeks by the shutdown and the field period extended |
| **Data Quality** | **High Risk** | Quarterly early releases cut to biannual; gender identity items removed (2025); major granularity reduction formally proposed for 2028 |
| **Statutory Context** | **No Known Issue** | Explicit PHS Act §306 mandate; required for Healthy People/HHS reporting; no substitute exists |
| **Staffing and Funding** | **Moderate Risk** | ~10% staff lost by fall 2025; ~25% RIF attempted and rescinded; FY26 budget proposes ~9% further FTE cut; reorganization threatened |
| **Policy** | **High Risk** | EO 14168-driven ICR changes already removed content; dissemination subject to direct political intervention |

**Overall interpretation:** NHIS is *not* at imminent risk of termination — its statutory foundation, active ICR, on-schedule releases, and role as infrastructure for other federal programs (MEPS, Healthy People) are strong stabilizers. The risk profile is concentrated in **erosion rather than elimination**: content removal aligned with administration priorities, reduced release frequency, a proposed 2028 redesign that trades detail for cost savings, and a workforce shown to be one budget cycle away from a 25% cut. For preservation purposes, the highest-priority actions are mirroring the complete historical archive (FTP + documentation), archiving pre-2025 instruments containing gender identity items, and capturing 2019–2027 detailed questionnaire content before the 2028 redesign takes effect.
